claims.text: Structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by competition between configurational entropy and favorable atomic-pair interactions.
Specific favorable atomic-pair interactions induce short-range chemical order.
Local short-range chemical order pins the alloy structure and suppresses phase segregation at elevated temperature.
The initial nanoalloy is a metastable, approximately equiatomic single phase.
The initial nanoalloy has a largely random atomic distribution with incipient specific-pair clustering.
Changing the concentration of an ordering-promoting element can weaken or strengthen specific pair interactions.
Al–Ni pairing can produce short-range chemical order in Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni high-entropy alloys.
Co–Cr pairing is an example of an attractive interaction that produces localized clustering in the proposed nanoalloy.
High mixing entropy favors a uniform, disordered solid solution.
Specific interatomic pair interactions drive local chemical ordering.
At elevated temperature, thermal energy reduces ordering kinetics.
Once nanoscale ordered domains form, they act as pinning centers that preserve a single phase against segregation or phase transformation.
Reducing the propensity for strong pair interactions will produce less local clustering after high-temperature annealing.
Reducing the propensity for strong pair interactions will produce a more uniform annealed structure than the baseline alloy.
An unmodified equiatomic high-entropy alloy can exhibit measurable short-range order under high-temperature conditions.
The prediction is limited to particles tens of nanometers in size annealed at approximately 800–1000 °C while remaining solid.
The prediction may not apply to bulk alloys.
Near the melting point, full chemical disordering occurs and the prediction may fail.
Surface-energy effects may influence structural and chemical stability in these nanoalloys.
Composition-dependent short-range chemical order is associated with B2 phase formation in Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism say that short-range ordered domains stabilize the single-phase structure and suppress segregation, whereas the predicted outcome presents weakening those interactions and diminishing that order as producing a more uniform structure. The direction expected for phase stability or segregation after removing the proposed pinning mechanism is therefore internally inconsistent.

The conditions characterize 800–1000 °C as sufficient for significant thermal fluctuations and activated atomic motion, while the mechanism says elevated-temperature thermal energy reduces ordering kinetics. No explanation is given for how increased mobility reduces kinetics rather than reducing equilibrium order or accelerating rearrangement.
